claim: Pyphe is an all-in-one solution for automating and improving data analysis pipelines associated with large-scale fitness screens.
source: We present an all-in-one solution, pyphe, for automating and improving data analysis pipelines associated with large-scale fitness screens, including image acquisition and quantification, data normalisation, and statistical analysis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the pyphe tool.

claim: Pyphe processes fitness data from colony sizes, viability scores from phloxine B staining, or colony growth curves.
source: Pyphe is versatile and processes fitness data from colony sizes, viability scores from phloxine B staining or colony growth curves, all obtained with inexpensive transilluminating flatbed scanners.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract describing the capabilities of pyphe.

claim: The fitness information contained in late endpoint measurements of colony sizes is similar to maximum growth slopes from time series.
source: We apply pyphe to show that the fitness information contained in late endpoint measurements of colony sizes is similar to maximum growth slopes from time series.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Colony size and viability provide complementary, independent information.
source: We phenotype gene-deletion strains of fission yeast in 59,350 individual fitness assays in 70 conditions, revealing that colony size and viability provide complementary, independent information.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3A showing weak correlation (r = −0.088).

claim: Viability scores obtained from quantifying the redness of phloxine-stained colonies accurately reflect the fraction of live cells within colonies.
source: Viability scores obtained from quantifying the redness of phloxine-stained colonies accurately reflect the fraction of live cells within colonies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging flow cytometry data in Figure 4D showing correlation (r = −0.88).

claim: Pyphe is user-friendly, open-source and fully documented.
source: Pyphe is user-friendly, open-source and fully documented, illustrated by applications to diverse fitness analysis scenarios.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the software characteristics.

claim: The availability of knock-out libraries has revolutionised reverse genetics and enabled the field of functional genomics.
source: The availability of knock-out libraries has revolutionised reverse genetics and enabled the field of functional genomics (Giaever and Nislow, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Large collections of wild isolates have proven a powerful tool to study complex traits.
source: Simultaneously, large collections of wild isolates (Jeffares et al., 2015; Peter et al., 2018), as well as synthetic populations (Bloom et al., 2013; Cubillos et al., 2013), have proven a powerful tool to study complex traits.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Synthetic populations have proven a powerful tool to study complex traits.
source: Simultaneously, large collections of wild isolates (Jeffares et al., 2015; Peter et al., 2018), as well as synthetic populations (Bloom et al., 2013; Cubillos et al., 2013), have proven a powerful tool to study complex traits.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The systematic measurement of fitness for hundreds of conditions and/or hundreds/thousands of strains in parallel is driving systems-level understanding of gene function.
source: More recently, the systematic measurement of fitness for hundreds of conditions and/or hundreds/thousands of strains in parallel is driving our systems-level understanding of gene function (Brochado et al., 2018; Costanzo et al., 2016; Kuzmin et al., 2018; Nichols et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Microbial phenomics screens generally follow a workflow where strains are arranged in high-density arrays.
source: Microbial phenomics screens generally follow a workflow where strains are arranged in high-density arrays (e.g. 384 or 1536 colonies per plate) and transferred using a colony-pinning robot or manual replicator.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of standard practice.

claim: Image analysis software enables fast and precise quantification of colony sizes and other phenotypes.
source: Image analysis software enables fast and precise quantification of colony sizes and other phenotypes (Bischof et al., 2016; Kritikos et al., 2017; Lawless et al., 2010; Memarian et al., 2007; Wagih and Parts, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Colony-size data is prone to noise and technical variation between areas on the same plate and across plates and batches.
source: Colony-size data is prone to noise and technical variation between areas on the same plate and across plates and batches, some of which can be corrected by normalisation procedures (Baryshnikova et al., 2010; Blomberg, 2011; Zackrisson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Normalisation procedures can correct some noise and technical variation in colony-size data.
source: Colony-size data is prone to noise and technical variation between areas on the same plate and across plates and batches, some of which can be corrected by normalisation procedures (Baryshnikova et al., 2010; Blomberg, 2011; Zackrisson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Specialised approaches are available for assessing differential fitness statistically.
source: Finally, differential fitness is assessed statistically, for which specialised approaches are available (Collins et al., 2010; Collins et al., 2006; Wagih and Parts, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Most screens use a single image or timepoint per plate (an endpoint measurement).
source: Most screens use a single image or timepoint per plate (an endpoint measurement).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of common practice.

claim: Potentially more information is contained in the growth of colony sizes over time.
source: Potentially more information is contained in the growth of colony sizes over time and a low-resolution time course of colony sizes can be used to fit growth models to population size data (Addinall et al., 2011; Banks et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: A low-resolution time course of colony sizes can be used to fit growth models to population size data.
source: Potentially more information is contained in the growth of colony sizes over time and a low-resolution time course of colony sizes can be used to fit growth models to population size data (Addinall et al., 2011; Banks et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: High-resolution image time series have been used to determine lag phases.
source: High-resolution image time series contain potentially even more information and have been used to determine lag phases (Levin-Reisman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Highly precise fitness determination has been achieved by high-resolution, transilluminating time course imaging and growth curve analysis.
source: Recently, highly precise fitness determination has been achieved by high-resolution, transilluminating time course imaging and growth curve analysis (Takeuchi et al., 2014) and combined with a reference grid normalisation (Zackrisson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The parallel use of commercially available scanners, combined with high-density arrays of colonies can enable growth curve-based phenotyping at very large scales.
source: The parallel use of commercially available scanners, combined with high-density arrays of colonies can enable growth curve-based phenotyping at very large scales, but poses challenges in terms of data storage, processing, equipment and the need for temperature-controlled space.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation about current capabilities and challenges.

claim: Growth curve-based phenotyping at very large scales poses challenges in terms of data storage, processing, equipment and the need for temperature-controlled space.
source: The parallel use of commercially available scanners, combined with high-density arrays of colonies can enable growth curve-based phenotyping at very large scales, but poses challenges in terms of data storage, processing, equipment and the need for temperature-controlled space.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation about challenges.

claim: The dead-cell stain phloxine B can provide an additional phenotypic readout related to the proportion of dead cells in a colony.
source: The dead-cell stain phloxine B can provide an additional phenotypic readout related to the proportion of dead cells in a colony.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of phloxine B functionality.

claim: Phloxine B has been used to assess the viability of cells in budding yeast by microscopy.
source: Phloxine B has been used to assess the viability of cells in budding yeast by microscopy (Tsukada and Ohsumi, 1993) and in fission yeast colonies (Matynia et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Phloxine B has been used to assess the viability of cells in fission yeast colonies.
source: Phloxine B has been used to assess the viability of cells in budding yeast by microscopy (Tsukada and Ohsumi, 1993) and in fission yeast colonies (Matynia et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: When applied in a screening context, colonies are assigned a score which reflects the 'redness' of the colony to serve as an additional quantitative phenotype.
source: When applied in a screening context, colonies are assigned a score which reflects the 'redness' of the colony to serve as an additional quantitative phenotype that can be used for downstream analysis (Lie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: A consensus data framework for microbial colony screens has not emerged.
source: Despite the popularity and importance of microbial colony screens, a consensus data framework has so far not emerged.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation about the field.

claim: Pyphe consists of 6 command-line tools, each performing a different workflow step.
source: Pyphe (python package for phenotype analysis) consists of 6 command-line tools, each performing a different workflow step as well as the underlying functions, provided as a python package to expert users.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of pyphe's structure.

claim: The pyphe pipeline is designed to take different fitness proxies as input: endpoint colony sizes, colony growth curves or endpoint colony viability estimates from phloxine B staining.
source: The pyphe pipeline is designed to take different fitness proxies as input: endpoint colony sizes, colony growth curves or endpoint colony viability estimates from phloxine B staining (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Image acquisition, image analysis, growth-curve analysis, data normalisation and statistical analysis are split into separate tools in pyphe.
source: Image acquisition, image analysis, growth-curve analysis, data normalisation and statistical analysis are split into separate tools which can be assembled into a pipeline as required for each experiment and combined with other published tools, e.g. gitter (Wagih and Parts, 2014) for image quantification.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pyphe's modular design.

claim: Each pyphe tool takes and produces human-readable data in text/table format.
source: Each tool takes and produces human-readable data in text/table format.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pyphe's data format.

claim: Pyphe-scan provides an interface for image acquisition using SANE (Scanner Access Now Easy) on a Linux-type operating system.
source: In a typical workflow, images are acquired using pyphe-scan which provides an interface for image acquisition using SANE (Scanner Access Now Easy) on a Linux-type operating system.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pyphe-scan functionality.

claim: Pyphe-scan handles plate numbering, cropping and flopping, and format conversion functionality for large image stacks.
source: It handles plate numbering, cropping and flopping, and format conversion functionality for large image stacks.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pyphe-scan functionality.

claim: Pyphe-scan was written to work with EPSON V800 scanners.
source: Pyphe-scan was written to work with EPSON V800 scanners, the newer model in the series previously used by others (Takeuchi et al., 2014; Zackrisson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous work using similar scanners.

claim: Pyphe-quantify can operate in three different modes: batch mode, redness mode, and timecourse mode.
source: Colony properties are then quantified from images using pyphe-quantify which can operate in three different modes. In batch mode (for colony-size quantification using grayscale transmission scanning) or redness mode (colony-viability estimation using phloxine B and reflective colour scanning), it separately analyses all images that match the input pattern (by default all jpg images in working directory), producing a csv table and qc image for each. In timecourse mode, colony positions are determined in the last image and the mask is applied to all previous images, extracting background-subtracted sums of pixel intensities for each colony/spot and producing a single table with the growth curves (one per column).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pyphe-quantify functionality.

claim: Pyphe quantify reports a wide range of colony properties: colony area, overall intensity, circularity, perimeter and centroid coordinates.
source: Pyphe quantify reports a wide range of colony properties: colony area, overall intensity (an estimator that reflects thickness as well as area), circularity, perimeter and centroid coordinates, making this tool useful in cases where colonies are not arrayed.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pyphe-quantify output.

claim: Image pixel darkness is known to scale non-linearly with true colony thickness/cell number.
source: Image pixel darkness is known to scale non-linearly with true colony thickness/cell number (Zackrisson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Fitness estimates reported by pyphe-analyse are related but not strictly the same as cell counts.
source: Fitness estimates reported by pyphe-analyse are therefore related but not strictly the same as cell counts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the non-linear relationship between pixel darkness and cell number.

claim: The Scan-o-matic pipeline offers suitable calibration functionalities if absolute population sizes are required.
source: If absolute population sizes are required for an experiment, the Scan-o-matic pipeline offers suitable calibration functionalities (Zackrisson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Pyphe implements a grid normalisation procedure based on the one previously described by Zackrisson et al., 2016.
source: Pyphe implements a grid normalisation procedure based on the one previously described (Zackrisson et al., 2016) as well as row/column median normalisation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to the original method.

claim: Pyphe implements row/column median normalisation.
source: Pyphe implements a grid normalisation procedure based on the one previously described (Zackrisson et al., 2016) as well as row/column median normalisation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pyphe's normalisation methods.

claim: Both grid normalisation and row/column median normalisation strategies produce relative fitness estimates where a value of 1 corresponds to the fitness of the grid strain or the plate median respectively.
source: Both strategies produce relative fitness estimates where a value of 1 corresponds to the fitness of the grid strain or the plate median respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the output of normalisation methods.

claim: The main output of pyphe-analyse is a single long table, containing one row per colony, with all position-, strain-, meta- and fitness-data as well as details about the normalisation.
source: The main output is a single long table, containing one row per colony, with all position-, strain-, meta- and fitness-data as well as details about the normalisation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pyphe-analyse output.

claim: Pyphe-interpret produces summary statistics and p-values based on the complete data report from pyphe-analyse.
source: Finally, differential fitness is assessed using pyphe-interpret which produces summary statistics and p-values based on the complete data report from pyphe-analyse (Appendix 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pyphe-interpret functionality.

claim: Pyphe-interpret gives users the option to either test for differences between strains in the same condition or between the same strain in different conditions.
source: Pyphe-interpret gives users the option to either test for differences between strains in the same condition or between the same strain in different conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pyphe-interpret functionality.

claim: Testing for condition-specific growth effects compared to a control condition is the recommended option in pyphe-interpret.
source: The latter is the recommended option for testing for condition-specific growth effects compared to a control condition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a recommendation for using pyphe-interpret.

claim: Previous studies have reported that information from growth curves are more precise than endpoint measurements.
source: Previous studies have reported that information from growth curves are more precise (Zackrisson et al., 2016), but their acquisition requires substantially higher investment and produces large amounts of image data.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Acquisition of growth curves requires substantially higher investment and produces large amounts of image data.
source: Previous studies have reported that information from growth curves are more precise (Zackrisson et al., 2016), but their acquisition requires substantially higher investment and produces large amounts of image data.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about growth curve acquisition.

claim: Lower precision of endpoint measurements could be easily compensated by a higher number of replicates.
source: While lower precision could be easily compensated by a higher number of replicates, growth curves provide the additional advantage that they capture the entire growth phase instead of a static snapshot.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference about experimental design.

claim: Growth curves provide the additional advantage that they capture the entire growth phase instead of a static snapshot.
source: While lower precision could be easily compensated by a higher number of replicates, growth curves provide the additional advantage that they capture the entire growth phase instead of a static snapshot.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about growth curves.

claim: The fitness of a strain with a long lag phase but high maximum growth rate may be underestimated if an early timepoint is chosen for endpoint measurement.
source: For example, the fitness of a strain with a long lag phase but high maximum growth rate may be underestimated if an early timepoint is chosen.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a speculation about potential issues with endpoint measurements.

claim: Image time series were recorded for 57 S. pombe wild strains growing in 1536 spots per plate in approximately 20 replicates on 8 different media.
source: To assess the extent to which the choice of the timepoint matters, we recorded image time series for 57 S. pombe wild strains growing in 1536 spots per plate in approximately 20 replicates on 8 different media (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental setup.

claim: The 57 S. pombe wild strains are genotypically and phenotypically diverse and display a broad range of growth characteristics.
source: These strains are genotypically and phenotypically diverse and display a broad range of growth characteristics (Jeffares et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Relative colony sizes remained largely constant after the period of fast growth had come to end at roughly 16 hr.
source: Relative colony sizes remained largely constant after the period of fast growth had come to end at roughly 16 hr (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A correlation matrix of all timepoints showed near perfect correlation of timepoints with the 48 hr end point from 16 hr.
source: Concordantly, a correlation matrix of all timepoints showed near perfect correlation of timepoints with the 48 hr end point from 16 hr (Figure 2Biii).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2Biii.

claim: All timepoints were correlated with the initial timepoint, albeit much lower, suggesting a significant bias introduced by the amount of initially deposited biomass.
source: Notably, all timepoints were correlated with the initial timepoint, albeit much lower, suggesting a significant bias introduced by the amount of initially deposited biomass.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data with an inference about the cause.

claim: The bias from initially deposited biomass is more pronounced with wild strains than with knock-out collections as the former exhibit a variable degree of cell aggregation.
source: In our hands, this problem is more pronounced with wild strains than with knock-out collections as the former exhibit a variable degree of cell aggregation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the authors' experience.

claim: The bias from initially deposited biomass can be overcome by reporting strain fitness as a ratio of growth in an assay condition relative to a control condition.
source: However, we overcome this issue by reporting strain fitness as a ratio of growth in an assay condition relative to a control condition, in which case this bias is neutralised.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a solution to the bias problem.

claim: Later timepoints generally showed a much better correlation with maximum growth rate compared to early ones or those taken when growth is most rapid.
source: We next analysed image timeseries with pyphe-quantify in timecourse mode, extracted slopes with pyphe-growthcurves (Appendix 4) and applied grid correction in pyphe-analyse. Later timepoints generally showed a much better correlation with maximum growth rate compared to early ones or those taken when growth is most rapid (Figure 2 Bi+ii).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2 Bi+ii.

claim: Across all conditions, the median correlation of corrected maximum slopes with corrected colony sizes at the final timepoint was 0.95.
source: Across all conditions, the median correlation of corrected maximum slopes with corrected colony sizes at the final timepoint was 0.95 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Late timepoints should be chosen for endpoint measurements, when the readout is stable and correlates well with the maximum growth rate.
source: We conclude that late timepoints should be chosen for endpoint measurements, when the readout is stable and correlates well with the maximum growth rate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: For uncorrected colony sizes, the coefficient of variation (CV) of 96 replicates of the control strain dropped steadily during the rapid growth phase, reaching a minimum around 20 hr when it started to rise again.
source: For uncorrected colony sizes, the coefficient of variation (CV, ratio of the standard deviation to the mean) of 96 replicates of the control strain, dispersed evenly in the plate, dropped steadily during the rapid growth phase, reaching a minimum around 20 hr when it started to rise again (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The rise in CV after 20 hr is likely due to edge and other spatial effects which affect later growth as nutrients deplete and plates start to dry unevenly.
source: This is likely due to edge and other spatial effects which affect later growth as nutrients deplete and plates start to dry unevenly.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference about the cause of the observed pattern.

claim: After normalisation, the CV was generally lower, and the later rise in noise could be compensated so that the CV remained near its minimum.
source: After normalisation, the CV was generally lower, and this later rise in noise could be compensated so that the CV remained near its minimum.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about the effect of normalisation.

claim: The CV of the maximum slopes was lower than obtained with endpoints.
source: The CV of the maximum slopes was lower than obtained with endpoints.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: CV values alone are insufficient to judge the effectiveness of a normalisation strategy, as it reflects precision of the reported values but not the method's ability to delineate differences between strains.
source: However, CV values alone are insufficient to judge the effectiveness of a normalisation strategy, as it reflects precision of the reported values but not the method's ability to delineate differences between strains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological consideration.

claim: The fraction of unexplained variance (FUV) indicates the level of noise relative to the biological signal in the data.
source: As an additional indicator, we therefore used the ratio of the variance of the controls and the variance of the entire dataset, the fraction of unexplained variance (FUV), which indicates the level of noise relative to the biological signal in the data.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a definition of FUV.

claim: The FUV was at a minimum at around 20 hr for the uncorrected data.
source: Overall, the FUV behaved similarly to the CV and was at a minimum at around 20 hr for the uncorrected data.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: With corrections, the minimal FUV value was largely maintained until the end of the experiment.
source: With corrections, this minimal value was largely maintained until the end of the experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about the effect of corrections.

claim: A lower FUV can be obtained by using maximum slopes rather than individual timepoints.
source: A lower FUV can be obtained by using maximum slopes rather than individual timepoints.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: There is a danger that any normalisation strategy could create false positives.
source: Although correcting for position and batch effects is essential for high-throughput experiments conducted on agar plates, there is a danger that any normalisation strategy could also create false positives.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a concern about normalisation methods.

claim: A grid colony positioned next to a rapidly growing colony will be smaller due to nutrient competition, leading to underestimation of the expected fitness in that area.
source: Specifically, a grid colony positioned next to a rapidly growing colony will be smaller (due to nutrient competition), leading to underestimation of the expected fitness in that area which will further increase the fitness estimate of neighbouring colonies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation of a potential artifact.

claim: After reference grid normalisation, a (generally weak but detectable) secondary edge effect was often observed for colonies positioned in the next inward row/column.
source: Indeed, after reference grid normalisation, we often observed a (generally weak but detectable) secondary edge effect for colonies positioned in the next inward row/column (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The secondary edge effect can be remedied by an additional row/column median normalisation, if the majority of strains in each row/column has no growth effect.
source: We found, however, that this effect can be remedied by an additional row/column median normalisation, if the majority of strains in each row/column has no growth effect (as is usually the case when working with knock-out collections).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a solution to the secondary edge effect.

claim: For uncorrected fitness values, there was generally a positive correlation between colony size and the sum of its 8 neighbours, indicating that regional plate effects dominate over competition between neighboring colonies.
source: For uncorrected fitness values, there was generally a positive correlation (stronger for colony sizes than for slopes), indicating that regional plate effects dominate over competition between neighboring colonies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data with an inference about the cause.

claim: The positive correlation between colony size and the sum of its 8 neighbours was removed after correction.
source: This bias was removed after correction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about the effect of correction.

claim: No negative correlation was observed after correction, indicating that grid correction does not lead to any significant effect exaggeration.
source: Importantly no negative correlation was observed. We conclude that grid correction does not lead to any significant effect exaggeration.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data and a conclusion.

claim: 238 S. pombe single-gene deletion strains were characterized in 70 conditions in biological triplicates (n = 59,350 total colonies profiled, including controls but excluding grid colonies).
source: To investigate how colony size and redness relate, we used the pyphe pipeline to characterise 238 S. pombe single-gene deletion strains in 70 conditions in biological triplicates (n = 59,350 total colonies profiled, including controls but excluding grid colonies, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental setup.

claim: The two fitness proxies (colony size and redness) showed little correlation (Pearson r = −0.088) after correction.
source: The two fitness proxies showed little correlation (Pearson r = −0.088) after correction of colony sizes using the grid approach with subsequent row/column normalisation and correction of redness scores by row/column median normalisation only (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Many mutant-condition pairs showed a strong phenotype in only one of the two read-outs (colony size or redness).
source: Many mutant-condition pairs showed a strong phenotype in only one of the two read-outs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Noise levels of redness scores were very low (CV = 1.04%).
source: Noise levels of redness scores were very low (CV = 1.04%) and the biological signal strong (FUV = 7.83%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a quantitative measure of data quality.

claim: The biological signal in redness scores was strong (FUV = 7.83%).
source: Noise levels of redness scores were very low (CV = 1.04%) and the biological signal strong (FUV = 7.83%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a quantitative measure of data quality.

claim: The phloxine B redness scores provide robust, precise information on mutant fitness, and serves as a largely orthogonal and independent measure compared to the growth rate or colony size measurements.
source: We conclude that the phloxine B redness scores provide robust, precise information on mutant fitness, and serves as a largely orthogonal and independent measure compared to the (well correlated) growth rate or colony size measurements.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Measurements with and without phloxine B were performed in different batches and in different weeks to exclude that batch effects increase the correlation.
source: Measurements with and without phloxine B were performed in different batches and in different weeks to exclude that batch effects increase the correlation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental design.

claim: Within the 14 phenotype vectors measured in total, identical conditions with and without phloxine clearly and consistently clustered together.
source: Within the 14 phenotype vectors measures in total, identical conditions with and without phloxine clearly and consistently clustered together (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The median correlation for the 7 condition pairs with and without phloxine was 0.92.
source: The median correlation for the 7 condition pairs with and without phloxine was 0.92, which was substantially higher than that of all possible pairs from the 14 phenotypes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The main driver of the biological signal is the condition and not whether phloxine B is included.
source: We conclude that the main driver of the biological signal is the condition and not whether phloxine B is included.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: A single gene, the trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase tpp1, was identified as having a small slow-growth phenotype on rich media (ratio of medians of corrected colony sizes 0.89, padj = 0.028) and a moderate effect on minimal media (ratio of medians = 0.79, padj = 0.049) when comparing growth with and without phloxine.
source: This analysis identified a single gene, the trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase tpp1, as having a small slow-growth phenotype on rich media (ratio of medians of corrected colony sizes 0.89, padj = 0.028) and a moderate effect on minimal media (ratio of medians = 0.79, padj = 0.049).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from statistical analysis.

claim: Differential fitness should generally be assessed against a control condition also containing phloxine B to account for genotype-specific effects.
source: In order to account for such genotype-specific effects, differential fitness should generally be assessed against a control condition also containing phloxine B.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a recommendation based on the findings.

claim: Colony composition and viability status at the single cell level was determined using ImageStream flow cytometry across 23 samples obtained from colonies with varying redness scores.
source: We determined colony composition and viability status at the single cell level using ImageStream flow cytometry. Across 23 samples, obtained from colonies with varying redness scores (Figure 4A), phloxine B staining classified cells into three populations (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 4): live cells which showed a background level of staining, dead cells which were brightly stained, and lysed or damaged cells which showed no staining.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Phloxine B staining classified cells into three populations: live cells which showed a background level of staining, dead cells which were brightly stained, and lysed or damaged cells which showed no staining.
source: Across 23 samples, obtained from colonies with varying redness scores (Figure 4A), phloxine B staining classified cells into three populations (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 4): live cells which showed a background level of staining, dead cells which were brightly stained, and lysed or damaged cells which showed no staining.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The fraction of live cells (alive/(dead+lysed+alive)) was inversely correlated (Pearson r = −0.88, with some grouping of strains) with colony redness scores obtained with pyphe-quantify and row/column median corrected by pyphe-analyse.
source: The fraction of live cells (alive/(dead+lysed+alive)) was inversely correlated (Pearson r = −0.88, with some grouping of strains) with colony redness scores obtained with pyphe-quantify and row/column median corrected by pyphe-analyse (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The correlation of colony redness scores with the fraction of live cells was stronger than the correlation with the fraction of live and lysed cells (lysed+alive /(dead+lysed+alive), r = −0.78).
source: This correlation was stronger than the correlation of colony redness scores with the fraction of live and lysed cells (lysed+alive /(dead+lysed+alive), r = −0.78, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that lysed cells, while not stained in the FACS, do contribute to colony redness.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lysed cells, while not stained in the FACS, do contribute to colony redness.
source: This correlation was stronger than the correlation of colony redness scores with the fraction of live and lysed cells (lysed+alive /(dead+lysed+alive), r = −0.78, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that lysed cells, while not stained in the FACS, do contribute to colony redness.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the correlation data.

claim: The dye is not washed out in colonies, unlike in cells resuspended in PBS for flow cytometry analysis, which explains why lysed cells contribute to colony redness.
source: This is explained by the dye not being washed out in colonies, unlike in cells resuspended in PBS for flow cytometry analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation for the observed phenomenon.

claim: In wild-type cells, staining with phloxine B and LIVE/DEAD agreed closely (accuracy 99.3% using LIVE/DEAD classification as ground truth).
source: We next asked how well phloxine B staining agrees with a distinct, established dead-cell stain (LIVE/DEAD). In wild-type cells, staining with both dyes agreed closely (accuracy 99.3% using LIVE/DEAD classification as ground truth, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Phloxine B staining, combined with the pyphe imaging and analysis pipeline, provides a sensitive and accurate readout reflecting the proportion of live/dead cells in a colony.
source: We conclude that phloxine B staining, combined with our imaging and analysis pipeline, provides a sensitive and accurate readout reflecting the proportion of live/dead cells in a colony.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Corrected (relative) redness scores are globally uncorrelated to corrected colony sizes in endpoint measurements of S. pombe knock-out mutants.
source: Furthermore, we show that colony viability measured by phloxine B staining and image quantification by pyphe provides a largely orthogonal and independent readout to colony sizes, thus offering an additional trait for mutant profiling. Redness scores obtained with the pyphe pipeline closely reflect the number of live cells in the colony. We report that corrected (relative) redness scores are globally uncorrelated to corrected colony sizes in endpoint measurements of S. pombe knock-out mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: The simplest explanation for how colonies can show normal growth even though a substantial fraction of its cells is dead is that growth and death are temporally uncoupled.
source: The simplest explanation for how colonies can show normal growth even though a substantial fraction of its cells is dead is that growth and death are temporally uncoupled.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Growth and death do not seem to be temporally uncoupled for the knock-out mutants investigated.
source: While this does not seem to be the case for the knock-out mutants investigated, it might be the case in other scenarios, e.g. when working with wild strains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation from the data.

claim: Growth and death could be spatially decoupled, with a subset of cells dying without the overall colony growth being affected.
source: Similarly, they could be spatially decoupled. As not all cells in the colony are actively dividing, especially during later growth (Meunier and Choder, 1999), and potentially in stress conditions, a subset of cells could die without the overall colony growth being affected.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation with a citation to support the premise.

claim: The observed uneven distribution of redness within the colony supports the idea of spatial decoupling of growth and death.
source: This idea is supported by the observed uneven distribution of redness within the colony (which we currently do not capture with pyphe).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation supporting the speculation.

claim: Colonies could sustain normal growth if viability were sacrificed for growth rate.
source: Furthermore, colonies could sustain normal growth if viability were sacrificed for growth rate (Nakaoka and Wakamoto, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation with a citation to support the possibility.

claim: Colony redness analysis opens up new avenues of investigations, for example for high-throughput chronological lifespan experiments.
source: Colony redness analysis opens up new avenues of investigations, for example for high-throughput chronological lifespan experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation about future applications.

claim: It will be important to examine the relationship between redness scores and live cells if the proportion of live cells drops to very low levels as the redness signal may saturate.
source: It will be important to examine the relationship between redness scores and live cells if the proportion of live cells drops to very low levels as the redness signal may saturate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation about potential limitations.

claim: Potentially even more information may be contained in the distribution of dead cells within a colony, which is hard to describe quantitatively and not reported by pyphe-quantify.
source: Potentially even more information may be contained in the distribution of dead cells within a colony, which is hard to describe quantitatively and not reported by pyphe-quantify.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation about additional information.

claim: Pyphe is an all-in-one solution enabling image acquisition, quantification, batch and plate bias correction, data reporting and hit calling.
source: The pyphe toolbox and underlying python package provide a versatile pipeline for analysing fitness-screen data. Pyphe is an all-in-one solution enabling image acquisition, quantification, batch and plate bias correction, data reporting and hit calling.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of pyphe's capabilities.

claim: Pyphe is flexible and accepts growth curves and endpoint measurements as well as colony sizes and staining as input.
source: Pyphe is flexible and accepts growth curves and endpoint measurements as well as colony sizes and staining as input.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of pyphe's versatility.

claim: Pyphe functionality is provided in the form of multiple separate, simple and well-documented command line tools operating on human-readable files.
source: Pyphe functionality is provided in the form of multiple separate, simple and well-documented command line tools operating on human-readable files.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of pyphe's design.

claim: Pyphe is written for the analysis of extremely large data sets (thousands of plates, millions of colonies).
source: Pyphe is written for the analysis of extremely large data sets (thousands of plates, millions of colonies), and its modular design allows the easy integration of other, future tools and scripting/automatisation of analysis pipelines which aids reproducibility.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of pyphe's scalability.

claim: Pyphe's modular design allows the easy integration of other, future tools and scripting/automatisation of analysis pipelines which aids reproducibility.
source: Pyphe is written for the analysis of extremely large data sets (thousands of plates, millions of colonies), and its modular design allows the easy integration of other, future tools and scripting/automatisation of analysis pipelines which aids reproducibility.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of pyphe's design benefits.

claim: The spatial correction implemented in pyphe, based on that proposed by Zackrisson et al., 2016, is effective in reducing measurement noise without overcorrection.
source: We show that the spatial correction implemented in pyphe, based on that proposed by Zackrisson et al., 2016, is effective in reducing measurement noise without overcorrection.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings with a citation to the original method.

claim: Late endpoint measurements provide similar readouts to maximum slopes, but with lower precision.
source: Late endpoint measurements are shown to provide similar readouts to maximum slopes, but with lower precision.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Growth-rate measurements do not necessarily boost phenotyping experiments in the sense that they contain novel information.
source: First, our results show that growth-rate measurements do not necessarily boost phenotyping experiments in the sense that they contain novel information, while one can compensate for the reduced precision of end-point measures by measuring more independent replicates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: One can compensate for the reduced precision of end-point measures by measuring more independent replicates.
source: First, our results show that growth-rate measurements do not necessarily boost phenotyping experiments in the sense that they contain novel information, while one can compensate for the reduced precision of end-point measures by measuring more independent replicates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Little if anything is gained from precisely pre-defining incubation times of assay plates prior to scanning.
source: Second, little if anything is gained from precisely pre-defining incubation times of assay plates prior to scanning.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Plates can be simply incubated for longer (usually 2–5 days for fission yeast), especially if the assay condition slows down growth.
source: Instead, plates can be simply incubated for longer (usually 2–5 days for fission yeast), especially if the assay condition slows down growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a practical recommendation based on the findings.

claim: By using genetically and phenotypically diverse wild strains for these experiments, the study covered strains with diverse morphology and growth behaviour.
source: By using genetically and phenotypically diverse wild strains for these experiments, we covered strains with diverse morphology and growth behaviour.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of the experimental approach.

claim: The tight correlation between late endpoint measurements and maximum slopes may not hold true for other species of microbes.
source: However, we cannot exclude that this tight correlation does not hold true for other species of microbes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a caveat about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Colony area measurements obtained with pyphe-quantify are very tightly correlated with those obtained with gitter (r=0.9991).
source: All 144 images from the image time course of 57 wild strains in replicates in 1536 format were analysed with pyphe-quantify batch and with gitter using remove.noise=TRUE and inverse=TRUE settings. (A) Colony area measurements obtained with pyphe-quantify are very tightly correlated with those obtained with gitter (r=0.9991).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: In terms of absolute values, colony size estimates from pyphe-quantify are consistently lower than gitter, which is due to the default thresholding settings.
source: In terms of absolute values, colony size estimates are consistently lower which is due to the default thresholding settings.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption as an explanation for the difference.

claim: Mean pixel intensities (averaged over all pixels identified as belonging to the same colony) depend strongly on colony size (thickness).
source: (B) Mean pixel intensities (averaged over all pixels identified as belonging to the same colony) depend strongly on colony size (thickness). This signal quickly saturates as colonies become larger, as previously described by Zackrisson et al., 2016.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption with a citation to support the observation.

claim: Mean pixel intensity signal quickly saturates as colonies become larger.
source: (B) Mean pixel intensities (averaged over all pixels identified as belonging to the same colony) depend strongly on colony size (thickness). This signal quickly saturates as colonies become larger, as previously described by Zackrisson et al., 2016.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption with a citation to support the observation.

claim: A strong edge effect is clearly visible in mean uncorrected colony sizes across hundreds of plates.
source: (B) Left: Mean uncorrected colony sizes across hundreds of plates. A strong edge effect is clearly visible. This is removed by grid correction which introduces a much weaker secondary edge (right).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: Grid correction removes the strong edge effect but introduces a much weaker secondary edge.
source: (B) Left: Mean uncorrected colony sizes across hundreds of plates. A strong edge effect is clearly visible. This is removed by grid correction which introduces a much weaker secondary edge (right).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: The linear regression model for predicting missing corners had an R² of 0.96.
source: (C) Prediction of missing corners based on neighbours. Shown are predicted versus actual colony sizes for top left and bottom right corners (the training data) for an experiment comprising 375 plates. The linear regression model in this case was y = 1.24 * horizontal neighbour + 0.16 * vertical neighbour - 34. The R² was 0.96.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: Extremely small grid colonies can result in negative values for expected colony sizes.
source: (D) Extremely small grid colonies can result in negative values for expected colony sizes.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: Using maximum slopes instead of endpoints usually results in lower noise levels.
source: (A) Distribution of CVs and FUVs (based on 96 replicates of the control strain 972 evenly dispersed through the plate, normalised for spatial effects with grid correction) across 8 conditions. Using maximum slopes instead of endpoints usually results in lower noise levels.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: There is a strong row-dependent effect with colonies in the top and bottom rows showing increased redness in uncorrected redness scores.
source: (A) Median redness scores across 308 plates (covering 78 different conditions). Top left: Uncorrected redness scores as obtained with pyphe-quanitfy in redness mode. There is a strong row-dependent effect with colonies in the top and bottom rows showing increased redness.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: The row-dependent bias in redness scores can be removed with a row/column median normalisation.
source: This bias can be removed with a row/column median normalisation as implemented in pyphe-analyse, resulting in median corrected redness scores in the top right.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 caption as a description of the correction method.

claim: Raw redness scores vary between plates, with a major factor being whether the media is minimal or rich.
source: (B) Raw redness scores vary between plates. A major factor is whether the media is minimal or rich.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: Unlike for colony sizes, row/column median normalisation achieves comparable reductions in noise for redness scores as other correction strategies.
source: (C) CVs and FUVs across all 308 plates with the three different correction strategies explained above. The optimal choice of normalisation will vary acorss experiments, but unlike for colony sizes, row/column median normalisation achieves comparable reductions in noise.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: Phloxine B can be toxic if exposed to light.
source: Phloxine B can be toxic if exposed to light (Qi et al., 2011), so we tested whether phloxine B changes growth parameters by determining colony sizes for our mutant set in 7 conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The readout of corrected redness scores is stable from the point at which fast growth ends and remains tightly correlated for at least 24 hr.
source: Timepoints generally correlated well after rapid growth had ended for a period of at least 24 hr (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The CVs and FUVs of redness scores were stable over at least 24 hr after rapid growth ended.
source: The CVs and FUVs were stable over this time as well (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mutants with the strongest redness phenotype showed a clear and strong increase in redness during growth.
source: We identified a group of mutants with the strongest redness phenotype in the set (corrected colony redness >1.05). These colonies showed a clear and strong increase in redness during growth (Figure 5D), suggesting that here redness was not temporally decoupled from growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: For mutants with the strongest redness phenotype, redness was not temporally decoupled from growth.
source: These colonies showed a clear and strong increase in redness during growth (Figure 5D), suggesting that here redness was not temporally decoupled from growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The exact timepoint to determine colony redness is not that critical, as long as colonies are not growing rapidly anymore.
source: As for colony growth, we conclude that the exact timepoint to determine colony redness is not that critical, as long as colonies are not growing rapidly anymore.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: All colonies showed a background signal unspecific to the dye that increased with colony thickness during early timepoints.
source: In general, we do not recommend analysing images of young, small colonies for redness. All colonies showed a background signal unspecific to the dye and this increased with colony thickness. During early timepoints, we therefore detect an increase in raw, uncorrected redness (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Analysing images of young, small colonies for redness is not recommended.
source: In general, we do not recommend analysing images of young, small colonies for redness.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a recommendation based on the findings.
